                    ### Question
                    A 21-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of a 2-week history of progressive shortness of breath and intermittent cough with blood-tinged sputum. During this time, he has also noticed blood in his urine. He has no history of serious illness and does not take any medications. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 92/min, respirations are 28/min, and blood pressure is 152/90 mm Hg. Cardiopulmonary examination shows crackles at both lung bases. Urinalysis is positive for blood and results of a direct enzyme-linked immunoassay are positive for anti-GBM antibodies. The pathogenesis of this patient's disease is most similar to which of the following?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Henoch-Schönlein purpura
opb. Polyarteritis nodosa
opc. Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis
opd. Autoimmune hemolytic anemia
ope. Graft versus host disease

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The patient's positive anti-GBM antibodies indicate Goodpasture syndrome, which is characterized by both pulmonary hemorrhage and glomerulonephritis. This condition is distinct from Henoch-Schönlein purpura, which primarily involves skin, joints, and gastrointestinal tract, and is not typically associated with anti-GBM antibodies. While poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis involves renal pathology, it does not present with the same pulmonary symptoms or the specific autoimmune mechanism indicated by the presence of anti-GBM antibodies. Polyarteritis nodosa can involve both renal and pulmonary systems but is not directly linked to anti-GBM antibodies. Autoimmune hemolytic anemia and graft versus host disease do not align with the specific findings of this case. Therefore, the most similar pathogenesis to this patient's disease is Goodpasture syndrome, which is not listed as an option. However, the closest option based on the presence of renal and pulmonary involvement would be poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis, despite the differences in underlying mechanisms.
